title: Minneapolis Café That Offered Free Meals Protesting ICE to Close Permanently
excerpt: Modern Times Café, rebranded Post Modern Times, removed prices in January and barred ICE in protest at enforcement in Minnesota. Owner Dylan Alverson says he has exhausted every option and will close the 16-year-old business by the end of 2026.
body:
• Modern Times Café in Minneapolis, rebranded Post Modern Times, will close permanently by the end of 2026 after nearly 16 years in business.
  • Owner Dylan Alverson removed prices in January and offered free, donation-based meals to everyone except ICE, in protest at federal immigration enforcement in Minnesota.
  • Reader utility: the closure is a business decision announced by the owner, not a change in immigration law or ICE policy — the café reopened in August with prices restored and 25 free meals a day, and plans about two more months of operation and celebration before closing.
  • Alverson said he was operating at a “zero profit margin” by October, with waits of up to two hours and heavy strain on staff.

Modern Times Café, a Minneapolis restaurant that removed its prices and offered free meals in protest against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations in Minnesota, will shut down permanently by the end of the year, its owner has announced. The café, which rebranded as Post Modern Times earlier this year, had operated as a free and donation-based restaurant welcoming everyone “except ICE,” according to Fox News and The Times of India.

“For the last six years, I’ve been trying to prove that Modern Times can continue to exist,” owner Dylan Alverson wrote on social media on Saturday. “I’ve exhausted every option without compromising the core fundamentals that make Modern Times what it is.”

Context

Alverson announced the free model on Instagram in January, in response partly to the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti during heightened federal immigration enforcement in the state, the reports said. The decision was made after Pretti was shot and killed by Border Patrol agents. “We absolutely cannot go on as we have. I am sick of generating money for the soldiers in our streets and for a government that won’t protect us,” Alverson wrote at the time. “Effective tomorrow we are done making money for the fascists that occupy our city.”

The café operated without prices for about six months, then briefly closed in July. When it reopened in August, it restored prices but continued serving 25 free meals per day. By October, Alverson told The New York Times he was operating at a “zero profit margin” and hoped the model could inspire other establishments, according to Fox News and the New York Post. He acknowledged the process was taxing for staff and led to customers waiting up to two hours for a meal, about half of which were usually given for free. Neighbors also expressed concerns that homeless and drug-addicted people would take advantage of the offer, the reports said.

Impact and Analysis

For immigrant communities in Minneapolis, including Indian-American families and restaurant workers in the Twin Cities, the café became a visible local symbol of the wider argument over ICE operations — a business that tried to turn meal service itself into protest. Its closure does not change any family's immigration status, any enforcement operation or any right to seek help, and readers should not treat the announcement as a policy development. It is, on the facts reported, a small business reaching the end of a model its owner says he could no longer sustain without abandoning its principles.

Alverson himself pointed beyond his own café when asked about the closure. In a comment to Fox News Digital, he stood by his remarks and suggested the bigger issue was how many other independent restaurants were struggling. “I think a bigger question right now is how many independent restaurants are close to collapse?” he said. That question matters in cities where immigrant-owned and immigrant-staffed restaurants operate on thin margins, whether or not they take any public position on enforcement.

The reports also show the practical limits the experiment ran into: staff exhaustion, long waits, neighborhood complaints and a return to prices within months, even while free meals continued at a smaller scale.

What's Next

Alverson said he plans to spend the next two months celebrating the 16-year-old business and discussing ways for a business like his to continue. “The only way for places like Modern Times to exist in the future is to actively challenge the reasons why it can no longer exist,” he wrote. He has also spoken about creating a fundraising mechanism to provide hospitality that other restaurants could join, according to Fox News.

No successor business was announced. For local readers, the timeline is clear: the café is expected to close for good by the end of 2026, after the August model of priced meals plus 25 free meals a day. Anyone relying on those free meals should plan for that end date, since no other operator has been named in the sources.

nri_angle: For Indian-American families and restaurant workers in Minneapolis, a café that made meal service a protest against ICE is closing on a business timeline, not a policy one — its 25-free-meals-a-day program ends with the business by the end of 2026, with no successor named.
author: Diaspora Desk

items.event: Café reopened with prices and 25 free meals.
